articles.content: https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3 In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people. To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over. “Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.” Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched. Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook This is unusual in a country where 40 million adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where 76 percent of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church. Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s. In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.” Today, people aren’t as likely to read the Bible, think it’s the Word of God, or go to church . But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is moving up . “We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.” These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty. “We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.” Times Have Changed Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said . Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said . “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. “I’ve got a new couple that moved into my neighborhood a while ago, and I haven’t even seen them yet,” said Daniel Simmons, executive pastor of campuses and central discipleship at The Summit Church. This means equipping the congregation is more challenging—and important—than ever before. “Evangelism can be this thing that is so burdensome and guilt-driven,” said pastor Christian Gracia. He planted King’s City Church in Las Vegas in 2024 with around 80 people and has seen the church grow to more than 400. “People can feel like they’re not ready or not good enough at evangelism,” Gracia said. “They don’t always know what to say, and can feel like a terrible Christian because they don’t do it. And I always want to help them understand that’s not true.” Start with Leadership If church leaders want to create a culture of evangelism in their church, there’s only one place to start, said Warren, who has baptized 150 people in the last eight months. “Tell me 10 people that you’ve shared the gospel with over the last month or two,” he said. “Because if the leadership team is not doing that, then it’s just an aspirational thing and you’re not going to be able to sustain it. You need those ‘just the other day’ stories.” At Perimeter, they’re putting structure around this. This PCA megachurch in Atlanta was planted by a gifted evangelist, Randy Pope, in 1977. Over the years, they’ve seen thousands come to Christ. But last spring, during a staff training, Norris noticed the focus had slipped. “What we tend to do, if left unto ourselves, if church leaders aren’t constantly pushing, is default to what is comfortable,” he said. “Church becomes more about me and my comfort or what my children need. . . . If you don’t constantly keep pushing on evangelism, it’s going to become too big of a burden and people will stop doing it.” Perimeter Church has grown largely through evangelism / Courtesy of Perimeter Church He saw this during Perimeter’s two-day staff workshop: “It became a bit more evident that most of us aren’t making disciples,” he said. “I told them—starting with the executive leadership team all the way down—that their supervisor is going to begin asking them what’s going on in their personal ministry.” This isn’t quota-driven, like “How many times have you shared the gospel this week?” It’s more along the lines of “Who are you praying for who doesn’t know Jesus?” “How are you trusting the Lord to provide opportunities for you to share the gospel with that person?” And then, “Have you been able to have those conversations? If so, how have those gone? Is there anything I can be praying for?” Over at The Summit Church, pastored by evangelist J. D. Greear, similar conversations are taking place. “We only grew 2 percent this year—we have not grown much over the past few years,” Simmons said. “We did some real soul searching in the spring, and found that our people have lost that invitation culture.” So Summit staff are reminding themselves of their goals. “Every ministry needs to know how they contribute to reaching lost people with the gospel, including the ones that may not intuitively do it,” Simmons said. “We’ve got a strong prayer ministry here. How does prayer contribute to reaching lost people? They should know that. Our deacon ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people. Our small group ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people.” Preaching As leaders begin to share their faith, it’ll come out in their conversations: “Just the other day, I was talking to a guy . . .” This is especially powerful if it comes from the pulpit—and that’s only the beginning of how pastors can use their platform to encourage the spread of the gospel. In a recent sermon, Gracia talked about truth and morality, explaining ideas such as postmodernism and cultural relativism. Christian Gracia preaching at King’s City Church in Las Vegas in October 2026 / Courtesy of King’s City Church YouTube “We’re not trying to win arguments,” he told his congregation. “I’m not trying to give you ammo for the water cooler. I’m trying to help you understand the world you live in. I’m giving you names for the water you’re swimming in, and then trying to help you navigate it. There are actually great reasons for what you believe. And there are also people who are seeking better answers than they have.” The Sunday teaching is primarily for believers. articles.title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
articles.content: What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer. While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost. With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology. Now, with The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application , they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today. What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith? The Westminster Confession of Faith takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England. After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries. The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe, The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx) Why Another Commentary? The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by A. A. Hodge , G. I. Williamson, R. C. Sproul, and more recently Chad Van Dixhoorn have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful? The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church. Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rather than treating the confession merely as a historical artifact or an academic text, the contributors consistently demonstrate how its theology serves the life of the church. Readers are reminded that the confession was written not simply to settle theological disputes but to help the church understand and live out the whole counsel of God. This pastoral emphasis matters. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. The Westminster Confession was never intended to be a document we merely admire or defend. Its doctrines are meant to shape the faith of the church as we “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 1:3). This commentary is useful because it helps readers make that connection, showing not only what the assembly confessed but why those truths matter today. Faith with Roots As a pastor, I’m finding that one of the great needs of our day is a sense of rootedness. Many Christians are looking for something that will give them a deeper sense of stability and connection to the historic Christian faith, something that didn’t begin with the latest movement or cultural moment. They’re looking for something with roots. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. This is one of the gifts of the Westminster Confession of Faith. Its doctrinal roots have given generations of believers a lasting stability, keeping them grounded in the historic faith through waves of theological and cultural change. It doesn’t simply teach us what to believe; it roots those beliefs within the life of the church, connecting us to generations of faithful Christians who have confessed these same truths before us. The Westminster Confession helps us to see that we don’t have to find our footing in the Christian faith on our own. We receive the gift of learning from generations of believers who have gone before us, helping us see the riches of Scripture with greater clarity and confidence. This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries. May it help a new generation find joy in the riches of the Reformed tradition and pass them on with confidence to those who follow.
articles.content_zh: 改革意味着什么? 标签经常使用,但并不总是谨慎。 对某些人来说,它只是提到救赎的特定观点. 对其他人来说,它引起一种传统、一种文化,甚至一种美学。 然而,从历史上看,改革意味着更加富有的东西。 虽然没有一句话能捕捉到被改造后的传统的全部,但至少它意味着三件事:是圣经,是盟约,是忏悔. 圣经的权威支配着我们的神学,盟约神学提供了圣经的红发框架,历史的忏悔总结并捍卫了教会的教义信念。 移除其中任何一根支柱,失去对改革后的传统至关重要的东西。 改革神学院长期试图在所有三个领域为牧师和教会成员提供教具, 近年来,该校院士编写了大量关于"旧约"和"新约"和"盟约神学"等著作. 现在,随着《威斯敏斯特信仰的忏悔:对其历史、神学和适用的综合评论》,他们把注意力转向改革后传统的忏悔基础。 结果的一卷不仅试图解释忏悔的教义,还试图表明为什么忏悔神学在今天仍然对教会至关重要. 韦斯敏斯特对信仰的忏悔是什么? 威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔会取而代之的是威斯敏斯特大会(Westminster Assembly),这是1643年英国议会在政治与教会剧变深刻的时期召开的由100多位部长和神学家组成的集会. 大会的任务是建议对英格兰教会的学说,崇拜,政府和纪律进行改革. 经过五年多的认真的圣经研究和神学审议后,大会产生了"威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔"(Westminster Confession of Faith)和"更大规模和更短的卡特克主义". 近四个世纪以来,这些文件共同成为全世界长老会教会的理论基础。 然而,议会的影响远远超出长老会。 忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架。 因此,它的神学影响塑造了几代基督教会,浸信会等福音派基督徒. 这本书的编辑们正确地指出,《忏悔书》也具有普世性,因为它在17世纪被基督教会和特定浸信会广泛接受,因为两个不同的神学家群体根据他们的神学信念修改了供词,产生了"萨伏依宣言"(1658年)和"第二次伦敦忏悔书"(1689年). 因此,威斯敏斯特忏悔与长老会、基督教会和浸信会有关。 (二十) 为什么另作一评注? 威斯敏斯特的"忏悔"从未缺少评论家. 从17世纪起,牧师和神学家都撰文解释其神学. A. A. Hodge、G. I. Williamson、R. C. Sproul和最近的Chad Van Dixhoorn以不同方式为教堂服务。 因此,我们为什么需要关于供词的另一条评论,是什么使得这一条有用呢? 威斯敏斯特忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架. 首先,这不是一位作者的工作,而是学者的合作努力,他们的专业知识跨越了神学的几个领域。 这种宽度允许量从不同的角度对待供词,同时保持明确的目的一致。 每个贡献者都会为他所讲的一节带来特殊的专门知识,但该卷整体关注的是帮助读者理解忏悔及其对教会的意义. 第二,评注是自觉的放肆。 撰稿人不但没有将忏悔仅仅视为历史文物或学术文本,反而一贯表明其神学如何为教会的生活服务. 读者们被提醒,供词的写作不仅是为了解决神学上的争议,而且是为了帮助教会理解并活出整个上帝的劝告. 这种对牧业的重视很重要。 忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西, 威斯敏斯特的忏悔书 从来都不是我们只崇拜或捍卫的文件 它的教义意在塑造教会的信仰,因为我们“延续着永远交给圣徒的信仰”(Jude 1:3)。 这篇评论很有用,因为它有助于读者建立这种联系,不仅表明大会承认了什么,而且表明这些真理为何今天重要。 对根的信念 作为牧师,我发现我们这个时代的伟大需求之一是一种扎根感。 许多基督徒正在寻找一些能让他们更深刻地感受到基督教历史信仰的稳定与联系的东西, 他们正在寻找有根的东西。 忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西, 这是威斯敏斯特忏悔信仰的礼物之一. 它的理论根源使几代信徒获得持久稳定,通过神学和文化变革的浪潮,使他们建立在历史信仰的基础之上。 它不只是教导我们该相信什么;它把这些信仰植根于教会的生活之中,把我们与几代忠实的基督徒联系起来,他们向我们坦白了同样的真理。 西敏的忏悔有助于我们发现我们不必靠自己找到基督教信仰的基础。 我们接受从我们之前的几代信徒那里学习的礼物,帮助我们更清楚地、更自信地看到天经的丰富之处。 这一卷是邀请人们重新发现这一遗产,并找到对上帝忠诚的新鼓励,上帝在几个世纪中一直维持着他的教堂. 愿它能帮助新一代人在改革后的传统财富中找到欢乐,并充满信心地将这些财富传给追随者。

articles.title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
articles.summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
articles.summary_zh: 我听到它不止一次地说 : “ 如果教会完成了它的工作, 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教堂为他所在社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是非营利组织。 由于他知道上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他想让多个教会参与这个项目. 我建议他考虑成立一个牧师理事会,并集体雇用一名工作人员来管理合并方案的运作。
articles.title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
articles.content: I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.” For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the church do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project. I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place. While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor. If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up? Clarifying Terms and Roles I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. “Church” has more than one use in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources. Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation. When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them. Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands. Ordained or Emergent Institutions The family, the local church, and the government are ordained institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation. While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure: The command to work led to the formation of businesses. The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools. The command to care for the sick caused Christians to form the first hospitals. The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the formation of charities . The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries. This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “ sphere sovereignty ” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. A family may work without forming a business, but they’ll never raise a skyscraper. Most believers recognize that the bulk of emergent institutions are legitimate. No one says, “If the church did its job being hospitable, restaurants wouldn’t need to exist.” Similarly, I don’t hear a lot of people saying, “If the church cared for the sick, hospitals wouldn’t need to exist.” Businesses, schools, hospitals, and charities all work best when operated by believers in accordance with God’s precepts. But they don’t have to answer to a plurality of elders any more than they have to be structured like a family whose children must answer to their parents. Churches, Nonprofits, and Businesses Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. That’s why Paul instructs Timothy that the local church shouldn’t aid a widow who has a family capable of aiding her (1 Tim. 5:3–4). Without question, overeager nonprofits at times impinge on the core duties of a family or local church. But in general, emergent institutions are legitimate and complement the work of the government, congregation, and family. Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. The Bible acknowledges this by its support of businesses . While the command to work is ordained by God, Scripture nowhere defines a prescriptive business structure. Yet the employer-employee relationship is acknowledged as legitimate, and the institution as one that promotes human flourishing. Once for-profit entities aren’t viewed as a local congregation’s failure, the line between a kingdom-minded business and a kingdom-minded nonprofit becomes fuzzy. For instance, plenty of for- and nonprofit enterprises intentionally employ and disciple people who are difficult to employ. Surely the tax structure doesn’t determine the theological validity of the enterprise. Thus, claims like “God created the church; he didn’t create the pregnancy resource center”—while true in the most literal sense—don’t communicate much of value. It’s a bit like saying, “God made trees. He didn’t make your table.” My table is made almost entirely of trees. The table is a good thing for which I should be grateful to God. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. The more the church does its job, the more local congregations there will be, the more nonprofits there will be, and the more redemptive businesses there will be. The question isn’t whether the church should replace the parachurch but whether God’s people will faithfully build every institution needed to accomplish his will.
articles.content_zh: 我听到它不止一次地说 : “ 如果教会完成了它的工作, 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教堂为他所在社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是非营利组织。 由于他知道上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他想让多个教会参与这个项目. 我建议他考虑成立一个牧师理事会,并集体雇用一名工作人员来管理合并方案的运作。 他认为这对他的背景来说是可行的。 我不确定他是否意识到讽刺。 我当然是:我们刚刚重新发明了501(c)(3)非营利的变体,他一开始非常想避免它。 虽然在他的案件中对基于信仰的非营利组织特别过敏,但许多人在基本层面上接受了这一前提。 根据我的经验,这种情绪可能来自在非教会部工作的人和牧师。 如果我们理解教会是基督为推进"天国"而建立的核心机构,那么它是否如此地失败了,以至于我们需要一支辅军来支撑它? 我回答说教区并不存在, 它的存在是因为上帝的命令自然产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 证明从澄清条款开始。 教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 “教会”在《圣经》中有不止一种用途。 在某些情况下,它普遍描述了上帝的人民(Matt. 16:15–18;Eph. 1:22–23;Col. 1:18)。 在其他情况下,它是一个具有上帝设定参数的地方教会机构,围绕它的运作(1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3: 1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “教会”一般是指为有需要的人服务或提供福音和门徒资源的基于信仰的非营利组织。 当然,作为普世教会的一部分,所有上帝的人民在推进上帝的使命方面都具有同等的地位,无论是作为护士、学生、牧师还是帐篷匠(见第18:1至3号法案)。 诚然,所有上帝的信徒不应该只参加,而应该对能够形成精神的当地教会负责。 在没有集合的时候,真主的宗族将担负许多任务,从管理创造到为被压迫者寻求正义。 我们可以作为个人完成这些任务,但建立或加入专门履行这些任务的机构往往是合理的。 这让我们到了一个关键点:真主专门规定一些制度,有些制度是从真主的命令中有机地出现的。 组织或应急机构 家庭、地方教会和政府是法定机构。 《圣经》为每个指定机构提供了一些指导,但也为解释留下了很大余地。 尽管这些指定机构对所有人来说都是必要的,但它们不足以最充分地执行上帝的众多命令。 因此,有些机构产生于指挥部,而不是一个公开的体制结构: 工作指挥导致了企业的形成. 将知识传给后人的命令导致了学校的形成. 照顾病人的命令使得基督徒组成了第一批医院. 照顾穷人、寡妇、孤儿和陌生人的命令导致了慈善机构的成立。 使各国门徒的指挥导致了传教板,出版社,和圣经翻译部. 这一规定性的区别与亚伯拉罕·库伊珀的 " 领域主权 " 相似,因为它承认了《圣经》中没有明确阐述的机构。 许多这些命令在较低程度上可以由指定机构执行,但有一些限制。 一家人可以工作而不创业, 大多数信徒承认,大多数新兴机构是合法的。 没有人会说,“如果教会做好了自己的工作, “如果教会照顾病人, 医院就不需要存在。 企业、学校、医院和慈善机构在由信徒按照上帝的戒律运作时都做得最好。 也不必像家庭一样, 子女必须向父母负责。 教会、非营利和经商机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。 这就是为什么保罗指示蒂莫西,当地教会不应该帮助一个有家庭能力帮助她的寡妇(1 Tim. 5:3–4). 毫无疑问,过度的非营利组织有时会损害家庭或地方教会的核心职责。 但总的来说,新兴机构是合法的,是对政府,会众和家庭工作的补充. 法定机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。 《圣经》通过支持企业来承认这一点。 虽然工作命令由上帝下达,但《圣经》却无一规定一种规范的商业结构。 然而,雇主与雇员的关系被公认为合法,而这种关系是促进人类繁荣的机构。 一旦盈利实体不被视为当地众会的失败,一个有王国意识的企业和有王国意识的非营利之间的界线就会变得模糊不清。 例如,许多营利和非营利企业有意雇用难以雇用的人和门徒。 当然,税收结构并不决定企业的神学有效性。 因此,“上帝创建了教会;他没有创建孕期资源中心”之类的说法,尽管从最直白的意义上讲是真实的,但并没有传达多少价值。 这有点像“上帝造出树木。 他没有给你做桌子。 我的桌子几乎是树做的 桌子是件好事 我该感谢上帝 教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 教会的工作越多,当地的会会越多,非盈利性会越多,而红发会的企业也就越多. 问题不在于教会是否应该取代教区,

articles.title_zh: 在我的架子上： L. Michael Morales的生活和书籍
articles.content: On My Shelf helps you get to know various writers through a behind-the-scenes glimpse into their lives as readers. I asked L. Michael Morales—professor at Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary and author of Exodus Old and New: A Biblical Theology of Redemption —about what’s on his bedside table, his favorite fiction, the books he regularly revisits, and more. What’s on your nightstand right now? Malcolm Guite’s Galahad and the Grail . Myths of origin hold potential for shaping a society’s culture and character. I believe Guite, aside from writing good poetry and a national epic, is endeavoring to reawaken (or refound) England to her rich Christian heritage. This volume is the first of a projected four-volume work that may well represent the new definitive collection of Arthurian legends. Writings of the Ramban , translated and annotated by Charles B. Chavel. Nachmanides is my favorite medieval Jewish exegete and commentator, and these essays illumine his character and offer gleaming gems of insight. His essay on redemption, for example, gives a nuanced understanding of eschatology in the Hebrew Scriptures. He argues convincingly that the exile threatened in Leviticus relates to the Babylonian exile that occurred in Jeremiah’s day, whereas exile in Deuteronomy uses more eschatological language and seems to relate to the exile after the Second Temple’s destruction. Another essay records his Disputation in Barcelona, when Nachmanides was forced by the Spanish government to engage in debate with a Jewish Christian convert. The disputation eventually led to his exile from Spain since, as one of the intellectual giants of his era, he acquitted himself overly well. (Christian readers will, for the most part, be disappointed with the representation of our faith by his opponent, but the disputation is helpful in that it offers insights into the sort of questions about the Messiah we should think about more deeply.) What are your favorite fiction books? Aside from literary classics, I enjoy mystery books, especially medieval mysteries, although it’s hard to find good ones. Ellis Peters’s Brother Cadfael series is good, although aimed for a younger audience (and so a bit tame). She had a beautifully poetic sense of providence and justice, which makes for satisfying conclusions. I also appreciate the espionage genre, such as the early works of John le Carré, like The Spy Who Came in from the Cold , A Small Town in Germany , and Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy . Perhaps less thoughtful but often more fun, Alistair MacLean’s books never fail to offer a little escape into adventure. What biographies or autobiographies have most influenced you and why? Iain H. Murray’s two-volume biography of D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones had a profound impact on me as a young, inexperienced pastor—my copies are filled with underlining and scribbled notes. This account of the Doctor’s life and ministry not only led me onto the paths of the Reformed faith, but demonstrated God’s blessings on a faithful minister’s diligent commitment to the ordinary means of grace, to prayer and preaching. Many of the problems and challenges facing the wider evangelical church when I was pastoring had their roots in the era of Lloyd-Jones’s ministry, so reading his biography offered much-needed biblical wisdom and the discernment of hindsight. Augustine’s Confessions is also a treasured book—it’s so personal and honest, and displays the sure and gracious hand of God in one’s life. Confessions is also about Augustine’s mother, Monica, and how she persevered in prayer on his behalf; and about God’s faithfulness and goodness in answering her prayers so abundantly. Throughout the book, readers also get fascinating glimpses of life in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. What are some books you regularly reread and why? Aside from regular Bible reading, it’s a challenge to reread many books, since my research-reading stacks are always waiting. Classics and modern classics, however, grow with you, so I prioritize these. Recently, I reread Sophocles’s Oedipus Cycle (actually, I listened to audio versions on my commute). Dante’s Divine Comedy —the Anthony Esolen or Robert and Jean Hollander translations—is the work I return to most, because I often find my soul needs to retake the journey, following in the Messiah’s footsteps from his passion to the resurrection. The historian Philip Schaff referred to Dante as an early reformer, which I think is true, even if we (Protestants) would still object to many aspects of Roman Catholicism in Divine Comedy (like Mariology and purgatory). There are still so many profound biblical lessons and theological truths that make Dante a spiritually profitable read. The Heidelberg Catechism and Calvin’s Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life are also worth rereading regularly, providing both comfort and conviction. What books have most profoundly shaped how you serve and lead others for the sake of the gospel? Early on it was books on the life and ministry of the apostle Paul, like Robert L. Reymond’s Paul: Missionary Theologian . Lately, given the focus of my research and writing, it’s been the life of Moses, especially through my commentary work on the book of Numbers. Both Moses and Paul labored tirelessly, sacrificially, and with much opposition, and by God’s grace they finished their race as faithful servants looking to the Lord in hope. Paul uses vivid sacrificial imagery to capture the life of ministry, that he was being poured out as a drink offering to God (Phil. 2:17; 2 Tim. 4:6). What a wonderful and devotional way to view being spent for his kingdom. When I was a pastor I also devoured Christian History magazines . Reading about the weighty and vigorous labors of others, whether John Wesley, John Newton, Oswald Chambers, Chrysostom, or William Wilberforce, was an inspiration and encouragement to persevere in my own labors (which, by comparison, were quite minimal!). What’s one book you wish every would pastor read? Although it’s not pleasant reading, I think every pastor should read (for starters) Stan Telchin’s Abandoned or Michael Brown’s Our Hands Are Stained with Blood . Christians are woefully ignorant about some of the blots on our history regarding our relations with the Jewish people, a tragic misrepresentation of Jesus and regrettable stumbling block to the gospel. Sadly, there is also a lack of prayer for the Jewish people offered up from our pulpits, which runs contrary to the hope expressed by many of our leading lights historically, such as Charles Haddon Spurgeon and Robert Murray M’Cheyne, not to mention the apostle Paul (Rom. 9:1–5). This was not always the case, and Scottish Presbyterianism in particular has a delightful history of collegial relations with our Jewish friends. On this point, I’d commend the book Time for Favour by John Stuart Ross. Part of the larger narrative, whereby the candle of the church’s heart for Jewish people has been quite snuffed out (at least in Reformed circles), is that a shallow apprehension of the Hebrew Scriptures has led to a flat biblical-theological understanding of redemptive history. Although they might not own the label, such “replacement theology” means, practically, that the church forgets about—or worse, disdains—Jewish people, which again is a terrible departure from both Scripture and the more refreshing eras of the church’s theology. There’s an appallingly pugnacious and high-handed antisemitism swirling in our world today, often fomented further by the media. This provides the church with an opportunity to pray and to repay our debt of love, which may be used by God to heal some old wounds. What’s your best piece of writing advice? For biblical and theological writing, I endeavor to write unto God as well as in the presence of God, that is, prayerfully. Beyond this, I’m the last one who should offer advice; writing is a hard and sometimes discouraging process for me, with a few moments of beauty
articles.content_zh: 《我的书架》帮助你了解各种作家, 通过幕后人物的一幕来了解他们作为读者的生活。 我问L. Michael Morales — — 格林维尔长老会神学院的教授和《出老而新:救赎的圣经神学》的作者 — — 关于他的床边桌子上的内容、他最喜欢的虚构故事、他经常重读的书籍等等。 现在睡台上有什么? 马尔科姆·盖特的加拉哈德和圣杯。 起源神话具有塑造社会文化和性格的潜力。 我相信Guite除了写好诗作和国史诗外,还努力使英国重新认识(或重新发现)她丰富的基督教遗产。 本卷是一出预测的四卷作品中的第一部,很可能代表了"亚瑟传奇"的新最终集. 由Charles B. Chavel翻译和注释的《拉姆班人》的著作。 纳克曼尼得斯是我最喜欢的中世纪犹太人的特质和评论家,这些散文照亮了他的性格,并提供了光辉的洞察力. 例如,他关于赎罪的论文对希伯来圣经中的空想学有细微的理解. 他令人信服地辩称,在利维提库斯受到的放逐与耶利米时代发生的巴比伦人放逐有关,而Deuteronomy的放逐则使用更多的宗教语言,似乎与第二圣殿被摧毁之后的放逐有关。 另一篇散文记录了他在巴塞罗那的争议,当时纳克曼尼得斯被西班牙政府强迫与一名犹太基督徒皈依者展开辩论. 争议最终导致他被流放出西班牙,因为作为他时代的知识巨头之一,他为自己释出过好. (基督教读者大多会对其对手代表我们的信仰感到失望,但争论很有帮助,因为它能让人们深入了解我们应该更深入地思考的弥赛亚问题。 ) 你最喜欢什么小说? 除了文学经典之外,我还喜欢神秘的书籍,特别是中世纪的神秘,尽管很难找到好的书籍。 Ellis Peters的"Cadfael兄弟"系列虽然针对年轻观众(也有点温柔), 她有着美妙的诗意感 天赐和正义, 这可以得出令人满意的结论。 我也欣赏间谍流派,如约翰·勒·卡雷的早期作品,如"从寒冷中进来的间谍"(The Spy Who Came in from the Cold),"德国的一个小镇"(A Small Town)和"丁克"(Tinker,裁缝,Soldier,Spy)等. Alistair MacLean的书中, 什么传记或自传 影响最大,为什么? Iain H. Murray的两卷自传D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones对我这个年轻、经验不足的牧师产生了深远的影响——我的书中充满了强调和写作的笔记。 这种对医生生活和牧师的描述不仅使我走上了改革后信仰的道路,而且表明上帝保佑一位忠实的大臣勤勉地致力于普通的恩典、祈祷和传道。 在我做牧师时,广大福音派教会所面临的许多问题和挑战都起源于劳埃德-琼斯部的时代,因此阅读他的传记提供了急需的圣经智慧和后视力。 奥古斯丁的忏悔书也是一本珍贵的书 -- -- 它非常个人和诚实,在一个人的生活中展现出上帝的坚定和仁慈之手。 忏悔的内容还包括奥古斯丁的母亲莫妮卡,以及她如何代表他坚持祈祷;以及上帝如此忠实和善良地回答她的祈祷。 在整个书中,读者也获得了第四世纪后期和第五世纪初生活的迷人一瞥. 你经常读什么书? 除了定期阅读圣经之外, 重读许多书籍也是个挑战, 然而,经典和现代经典随着你的成长而增长,所以我优先处理这些。 最近,我重新阅读了Sophocles的《Oedipus Cycle》(实际上,我在通勤时听了音频版本 ) 。 但丁的"神通喜剧"(The Divine Comedy)——安东尼·埃索伦(Anthony Esolen)或罗伯特(Robert)和让·奥朗德(Jean Hollander)(Jean Hollander)的译作——是我回归的大部分作品,因为我经常发现我的灵魂需要重新踏上旅程,沿着弥赛亚从他的激情到复活的脚步走. 历史学家菲利普·沙夫(英语:Philip Schaff)将但丁称为早期改革者,我认为这是正确的,即使我们(抗议者)仍然会反对神通喜剧中的罗马天主教的许多方面(类似"海洋"和"炼狱"). 仍然有如此多的深刻的圣经教义和神学真理使但丁在精神上有利可图地阅读. 海德堡卡德克主义和加尔文的"真正的基督教生活"金本册也值得定期重读,既提供了舒适又提供了信念. 是什么书最深刻地塑造了 你如何为福音服务 并领导他人? 早期是关于使徒保罗的生平和牧师的书籍,如罗伯特·雷蒙德的"保罗:传教神学家". 最近,鉴于我的研究和写作的重点,这是摩西的生活,特别是通过我关于"数字"一书的评论工作。 穆萨和保罗都坚持不懈地努力,不屈不挠地反对,在上帝的恩惠下,他们作为忠实的仆人,以望主而完成了他们的种族. 保罗用生动的牺牲形象来捕捉部会的生活,即被倒出作为献给上帝的饮料(Phil. 2:17;2 Tim. 4:6). 多么美妙和忠心的观赏 被花在他的王国。 当我是牧师的时候,我也吃过基督教历史杂志。 阅读他人的重心和强力劳动,无论是约翰·韦斯利,约翰·牛顿,奥斯瓦尔德·钱伯斯,克赖索斯托姆,还是威廉·威尔伯福斯,都是坚持自己劳动的灵感和鼓励(相比之下,这实在是微不足道了!). 你希望每个牧师都读一本书是什么? 或迈克尔·布朗的手被血染了。 基督教徒对我们历史上有关我们与犹太人民关系的污点感到悲哀无知,这是对耶稣的悲惨歪曲,是福音的令人遗憾的绊脚石。 可悲的是,我们没有为犹太人祈祷,这与历史上许多主要灯光,如查尔斯·哈登·斯普根和罗伯特·默里·姆谢恩,更不用说使徒保罗(9:1-5)所表达的希望背道而驰。 情况并非总是如此,苏格兰长老会尤其与我们的犹太朋友建立了友好关系。 我赞扬约翰·斯图尔特·罗斯的《时间倾斜》一书。 部分较大规模的叙事,即教会对犹太人的心灵的蜡烛被相当地吸出(至少在改革圈子中是如此),那就是对希伯来圣经的浅浅的担忧导致了对红色先发制人历史的平淡的圣经-神学理解. 虽然他们可能不拥有这个标签,但这种“替代神学”实际上意味着,教会忘记了——或者更糟糕的蔑视——犹太人民,这再次可怕地背离了圣经和教会神学中更加新鲜的时代。 当今世界上有一种骇人听闻的傲慢和高压的反分裂主义,常常被媒体进一步煽动。 这为教会提供了一个祷告和偿还我们相爱之债的机会,上帝可能利用这些债务来治愈一些旧伤. 你最好的写作建议是什么? 对于圣经和神学著作,我努力给上帝写作,以及当着上帝的面,即祈祷。 写作对我来说是一个艰难有时令人沮丧的过程,

articles.title_zh: 如何找到更好地利用工作时间的动力？
articles.content: I work for a property management company that oversees retail space. I haven’t been doing this very long, but I’m finding that I’m not as productive as I’d like to be. Often, entertainment and fear of failure keep me from working. How can I get motivated to use my time better? Given that we’re to submit to our earthly masters with sincere hearts as unto Christ (Eph. 6:5), our productivity at work isn’t ultimately about our advancement or our employer’s success—it’s about our gospel witness. From before the fall, God ordained our work for keeping, cultivating, subduing, and exercising dominion over his creation. We’re still called to that today in any work to which we set our hand—including the property management of retail space. As believers, all work invites us to leverage our God-given talents and strength to bless and bring order to God’s creation in order to glorify him. When alluring distractions or a fear of failure hinder our labor, we can turn to him who calls us for the truth that will rightly spur us on. Distraction of Entertainment When entertainment distracts us from working, we should start by counting the cost. If we’re spending work hours on entertainment and then have to finish our tasks in what should be our free time, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well? It may be infringing on our time for relationships, spiritual disciplines, or true rest. On the other hand, if our working hours are fixed regardless of how on (or off) task we are, such as a job we clock in and out of with responsibilities only while we’re present, why are we willing to steal from our employer by accepting their payment without exchanging it for the labor we promised? Maybe we need to “cut off” what’s tempting us by blocking entertainment apps on our phone and computer during the workday (Matt. 5:30). If we’re spending work hours on entertainment, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well? Once we do, how might we instead faithfully devote that time to our employer’s good, even being willing to go a mile beyond what’s expected of us (v. 41)? Maybe we provide the talking points requested for a presentation—but also organize them into slides to save someone else from having to do so. Maybe we address the three issues our leader ask us to correct—but also address two more we discovered in the process. Perhaps if we worked with this level of diligence and care, like Joseph with Potiphar, we’d be given increased responsibility and influence that could be leveraged for the kingdom. Those who can be trusted with little can also be trusted with much (Gen. 39:1–6; Luke 16:10). Certainly, God would be glorified as we work with all our heart as to the Lord and not to man (Col. 3:23). Fear of Failure When a fear of failure keeps us from working altogether, we can start by digging out the root of that fear. Do you fear that your limitations and propensity to error will keep you from succeeding? Acknowledge that inaction guarantees you won’t succeed, but attempts to succeed in the work God has entrusted to you allow the opportunity for his power to be made perfect in your weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). When you feel discouraged by your insufficiencies, trust God to provide the wisdom and strength necessary for the work to which he’s called you—by prayer (James 1:5), the edification of his Word, and your humble pursuit of correction and growth through helpful resources and the example of others. Do you fear others’ judgment when you fail? Remember that your purpose is ultimately to please God, not man, and that there’s no condemnation for those in Christ (Rom. 8:1; Gal. 1:10). When you make a mistake or fall short of what’s expected of you, admit your error, seek understanding about what to do differently, and move forward with the humility and resolve that may make others respect you even more than they did before. Trust God to provide the wisdom and strength necessary for the work to which he’s called you. Do you fear your identity being shaken because it’s dependent on your perfection in the workplace? Realize you’ll never be perfect at your work but that God’s grace is sufficient for your inevitable shortcomings and mistakes. Your identity is securely anchored in his perfection, not your own. You may see your paralyzing fear as a safety measure holding you back from failing. But how might your inaction be holding you back from succeeding? How might the Enemy be using that fear to steal your motivation, kill your endurance, or destroy your confidence in God’s promise to empower you? God has called us to be faithful stewards of all he has entrusted to us—investing our gifts and opportunities in efforts to multiply them rather than burying them in fear, thus proving ourselves to be good servants who will enter the joy of our master (Matt. 25:24–30). In all he has called us to undertake, our success will come not by our might nor by our power but by his Spirit (Zech. 4:6). In this we hope. For this we labor. By this we persevere. Work as God’s Workmanship Rather than wandering off into distraction or stalling on the path in fear of failure, we’re called to walk forward in the good works God prepared beforehand for us (Eph. 2:10). As we do, God may use our example to spur on coworkers, encourage leaders, or even compel the friends and family who witness our work to do the same with their own. In this way, we can take up the invitation to reflect our Lord, working with God-given courage and strength in all our labor, glorifying him who labors for us as we do.

articles.content: In the years since he was involuntarily committed to a mental health institution for bipolar disorder, Frederik deBoer has wrestled with both profound gratitude for a system that saved his life and also palpable frustration that his experience of healing has become so rare. All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered is the latest broadside from one of the internet’s most heterodox thinkers and writers. As an “old school” Marxist best known for writing The Cult of Smart , deBoer takes aim at how the cultural drift within his own tribe is responsible for making mental health care so elusive for those who need it most: “The tendency to treat mental illness as an exciting adventure, the endless romanticization of lunacy in popular culture, is one of many aggravations I have nursed for years” (8). The root of his aggravation—the treatment of mental illness and disability as an identity to be celebrated rather than a disability that needs treatment —isn’t all in his head. The use of talk therapy rose 47 percent between 2019 and 2024 . A 2025 LifeStance survey found around 29 percent of U.S. adults have self-diagnosed their mental health condition after consuming online content, rising to 50 percent among Gen Z (versus 9 percent of boomers). Of the people who self-diagnose symptoms, almost a quarter (24 percent) “rarely” or “never” feel the need to take the next step to discuss them with a qualified clinician. DeBoer argues that rather than reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, the inordinate attention given to the mildly and dubiously afflicted is a dangerous distraction crowding out help for the severely ill. Accelerated by social media, this “gentrification of disability” has become a full-blown social contagion, compromising even the experts and institutions responsible for mental health care (153–54). DeBoer is largely right, and the cultural shift he identifies has real-world implications both inside and outside the church. But the same ideological priors that so sharpen deBoer’s critique also suffer from two significant blind spots that, were they addressed, would make All in Your Head the more courageous, more constructive, and, therefore, more widely read manifesto we need. General Bipartisan Ire If you picked up All in Your Head to understand how modern therapy culture spread like wildfire across social media over the last several years, it’s not immediately obvious why deBoer starts his argument with an in-depth analysis of the anti-psychiatry movement’s influence in late 20th century politics and academia. But, if you can forgive me the pun, there’s a method to his madness. After a blistering critique of “rightwing libertarian” policies that neglected mental illness, he cashes in on the subsequent trust he earns with left-leaning readers to launch a series of absolute haymakers toward “a species of thought that sometimes amounts to a kind of leftist pseudo-radicalism or a libertarian fantasy” (198) that drives the “destabilizing . . . move from mental illness as reality to mental illness as symbol” (8). American individualism and anti-institutional bias aren’t new, but the painstakingly specific way deBoer traces their spread through the culture surrounding mental health and therapy is refreshing and instructive. Our “apolitical romanticism of resistance to modern society” fuels two opposite errors: On the right, mental illness is sometimes seen as either imagined or a symptom of weak character. But on the left, the same romanticism often describes mental disability as more en abling than dis abling, as if neurodivergent minorities don’t need society’s help—society needs theirs. Gentrification of Disability DeBoer’s emphatic rejection of this predominantly progressive error— of “making a medical disorder an identity”—is the “overarching principle of [his] book” (165). This is never more clear in what he labels “the gentrification of disability,” where “diagnoses become fads” because the “intellectual and discursive space once dedicated to the interests of the most afflicted have become fixated instead on a class of patients whose disorders range from mild to dubious” (154). Said spaces and institutions have become so compromised due to “the diseased incentives of social media” and “liberal conventional wisdom that says it’s offensive to question any claim any individual makes about a disability.” Combined, “we’ve created ‘disorder communities’” not unlike fan clubs “rooting for a particular sports team” (154). The disproportionate attention given to those wealthy enough or high-functioning enough to perform their disability online is a dangerous distraction with real consequences: The more that influential elites use their status to “define the disorder in the public mind,” the more those who are impoverished or severely disabled go unseen and neglected. The disproportionate attention given to those wealthy enough or high-functioning enough to perform their disability online is a dangerous distraction with real consequences. Clear to anyone not living under a rock for the last decade is how familiar these patterns are. As I argued in The Reason for Church , counterfeit institutions (e.g., social media) have bypassed gatekeepers and hijacked the incentives of vital social and spiritual institutions undergirding American life. All in Your Head won’t add many new tools for recognizing these patterns. DeBoer’s contribution is in tracing them throughout an often convoluted bureaucratic ecosystem from the perspective of a “crabby old Marxist” frustrated by the privileged hypocrisy of pop-critical theory and progressive politics. However useful, the same ideological priors also handicap his analysis with two glaring omissions. Incomplete Diagnosis and Insufficient Prescription His most obvious omission is the rapid rise of gender dysphoria diagnoses and sex-reassignment surgery for minors. For more than a decade, gender-affirming physicians have been telling parents they must choose between having “a trans kid or a dead kid,” but, as Rebecca McLaughlin points out , the evidence says otherwise: “Puberty blockers can make the mental health of some young people worse, not better.” Considering deBoer’s impressive track record of taking unpopular, heterodox positions within his own tribe, his failure to address what is arguably the most volatile and life-altering consequence of toxic therapy culture is bewildering. DeBoer’s second omission is more understandable. While he concludes with well-reasoned (if regrettably materialist and socialist) policy prescriptions, he doesn’t offer any remedy for the broader therapeutic culture (i.e., the “ideological commitment to radical individual autonomy” [77]) that he spends most of the book arguing is the root of resistance to reform. That neglect robs his policy prescriptions of much persuasive power. Christians can affirm deBoer’s diagnosis of the problem of individual autonomy, but the church has the social and spiritual resources missing from all legislative and policy prescriptions. We know humans were never meant to construct our identities but to receive them in Christ and through belonging to our families, to our churches, and ultimately to God. Church has the social and spiritual resources missing from all legislative and policy prescriptions. Despite any omissions, All in Your Head is a clear-eyed and validating read, especially for those in (or disappointed by) mental health care. It would be a fine complement to Matthew Loftus’s Resisting Therapy Culture and describes many of the downstream problems Philip Rieff anticipated in The Triumph of the Therapeutic . All in Your Head is “not a memoir” (8) but a pragmatic antimemoir seething with a holy discontent that challenges both performative mental illness and the also voyeurism that incentivizes it. 作为一位最以写作"聪明的邪教"而出名的"老派"马克思主义者,德博尔以自己的部落内部的文化漂移为目的,让那些最需要的人如此难以接受精神保健:"将精神疾病视为激动人心的冒险的倾向,在流行文化中无休止地浪漫化的放荡,是多年来我所照顾的诸多恶化之一"(8). 他的病情恶化的根源——将精神疾病和残疾视为一种值得庆贺的身份,而不是需要治疗的残疾——并不是他脑子里所有的东西。 2019年至2024年间,谈话疗法的使用率上升了47%. 2025年生活稳定调查发现,约29%的美国成年人在消费了在线内容后自行诊断出自己的心理健康状况,在Gen Z中上升到了50%(相对于9%的繁荣者). 在自我诊断的人群中,近四分之一(24%)的人“勉强”或“从未”感到有必要采取下一步措施,与合格的临床医生讨论这些症状。 但德布尔批评如此尖锐的意识形态前科也遭遇了两个重大盲点,如果这些盲点得到解决,将使你的头脑更加勇敢,更具建设性,因此,我们需要更广泛地阅读宣言。 一般两党爱尔兰人 如果你在脑海中看到现代治疗文化在过去几年里如何像野火一样在社交媒体上传播,那么DeBoer为什么以深入分析20世纪后期反精神病运动在政治和学术界的影响为出发点,这并不明显。 但是,如果你能原谅我的双关语,他疯狂是有办法的。 在对忽视了精神疾病的“右翼自由派”政策猛烈批评后,他依靠后来与左翼读者获得的信任,发动了一系列绝对的干草人,走向“有时相当于一种左翼伪激进主义或自由派幻想的思想”(198年),这种思想驱使“从精神疾病变成现实,转变为精神疾病作为象征”(8)。 美国的个人主义和反机构偏见并非新事物, 但DeBoer通过精神卫生与治疗的文化, 我们“反对现代社会的政治浪漫主义”助长了两个相反的错误: 在右边,精神疾病有时被视为一种想象或一种弱性症状. 但是在左边,同样的浪漫主义常常将精神残疾描述为比分身更困难,仿佛神经分身的少数民族不需要社会的帮助——社会需要他们的帮助。 对DeBoer残疾人的强烈反对,即 " 使医疗障碍成为身份 " 这一主要进步的错误,是 " 书中的首要原则 " (165)。 在他所谓的“残疾的基因化”中,这一点再清楚不过了,因为“曾经专为受感染最深的人的利益服务的智慧和模糊空间已经固定在一类疾病从轻度到可疑的病人身上”(154个)。 因为“社会媒体的有病刺激”和“自由传统智慧, 综合起来, " 我们创建了`混乱社区 ' " ,与粉丝俱乐部 " 为某一特定体育队 " (154个)不同。 对足够富有或高运作能力的人的过度关注, 有影响力的上层人士越是利用其地位“界定公众心中的混乱”,穷人或严重残疾者就越是被忽视和忽视。 对那些足够富有或高功用、足以在线处理残疾的人的过度关注是一种危险的分心,会产生实际后果。 过去十年里没有生活在岩石下的人很清楚 这些模式是多么熟悉。 假冒机构(如社交媒体)绕过守门人, 并劫持了影响美国生活的重要社会及精神机构。 在你的脑海中, DeBoer的贡献在于从一个被流行批评理论和进步政治的特有伪善所挫败的“疯狂的老马克思主义者”的视角来追踪整个经常被曲解的官僚生态系统。 不管多么有用,同样的意识形态前科也以两个明显的遗漏来阻碍他的分析。 未完全诊断和处方不足 他最明显的遗漏是性别障碍诊断和未成年人性转移手术的迅速上升. 十多年来,具有性别特征的医生一直告诉父母,他们必须在“一个跨性别的孩子或一个已经死亡的孩子”之间做出选择,但是,正如Rebecca McLaughlin所指出,证据却说道 : “ 纯洁的阻塞者可以使一些年轻人的精神健康恶化,而不是更好。 ” 考虑到德博尔在自己的部落内占据不受欢迎的、异性立场的令人印象深刻的记录,他未能解决毒害性疗法文化可能带来的最动荡和最改变生命的后果是令人困惑的。 DeBoer的第二次遗漏更让人理解。 虽然他最后给出了合理(如果令人遗憾的是唯物主义和社会主义)政策处方,但他并没有为更广泛的治疗文化(即“激进个人自主的意识形态承诺”[77])提供任何补救,他花在书中的大部分争论是抵制改革的根源。 这种忽视剥夺了他的政策处方 很大的说服力。 基督徒可以肯定DeBoer对个人自治问题的诊断,但教会在所有立法和政策处方中都缺少社会和精神资源。 我们知道人类从来就不是要建立我们的身份,而是要在基督中,通过属于我们的家庭、我们的教会以及最终属于上帝来接受他们。 教会在所有立法和政策规定中都缺少社会和精神资源。 尽管有任何疏漏,但《你的头脑》是一个清晰而真实的读物,特别是对于接受(或因)精神保健的人来说。 并描述了Philip Rieff在《治疗的凯旋》中预料到的许多下游问题。 你脑子里全是“不是回忆录”(8),而是一种务实的预言,充满了圣洁的不满,既挑战了表现性精神疾病,也挑战了刺激这种疾病的巫术。 结果是以令人印象深刻的解释对心理健康文化进行了具体和令人信服的再规划。

articles.title: How a Former Prisoner in Iran Wants You to Pray for Christians in Chains
articles.summary: Pray not only for what God might do for Christian prisoners in Iran but for what God might do through them, for his glory.
articles.summary_zh: 不久前,我和两名基督教青年在伊朗最困难的监狱之一服刑。 因为他们拒绝停止宣扬耶稣。 我问自己如何为他们祈祷, 他们说,“祈祷我们在这里的工作结束前不会被释放。 ” 他们带领许多同狱囚犯信仰。
articles.title_zh: 伊朗前囚犯如何希望你为被锁的基督徒祈祷
articles.content: Not long ago, I had a surreal phone call with two young Christian men serving prison sentences in one of Iran’s hardest prisons. They’re there because they refuse to stop preaching about Jesus. When I asked how I could pray for them, their answer wasn’t what you might expect. “Pray that we would not be released until our job here is finished,” they said. They had led numerous fellow prisoners to faith. Now, their chief concern was to remain inside long enough to disciple them. The call took me straight back to the five years I spent in prison for my faith. Now, these dear brothers (let’s call them Vahid and Reza) were behind bars, and I was outside. As we spoke, I pictured the wards and corridors, imagined the sounds and smells, and remembered how hard it was not to know how many years I would be there. But it was also an encouraging call. Vahid and Reza were in high spirits, talking about Bible passages that were sustaining them and how the Lord was at work. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. Their focus was the same as Paul’s in Colossians 4:3: “Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison.” Paul’s request wasn’t for an open prison door but for an open door for the gospel. Pray for Gospel Fruit Vahid and Reza’s request resonated with me. I remember being unable to pray for my own release. I tried on a few occasions, but I couldn’t open my mouth to ask the Lord to release me. If I’m following Christ, I cannot choose the path. I cannot choose the location. I should follow him wherever he goes. And as I followed him to prison, he brought beautiful fruit. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. I think of one prisoner, a devout Muslim, who was wrongly accused of spying for Iran’s enemies. He was praying he would be released and was frustrated to get no answer. He approached me one day, saying, “Farshid, our God is dead. But I’ve heard yours is alive. Will you pray for me?” Fearing it might be a trap, I took him quietly aside and prayed briefly in the name of Jesus: “Lord, you know this man. Please hear his prayer.” The very next day, the man rushed over excitedly and gave me a huge hug. That morning, he had learned his name had been cleared. He was released two weeks later. Our God is indeed alive. The Lord was also at work softening my parents’ hearts toward Christ during those years. I always say that even if only for the salvation of my parents, my time in prison was worth it. So, when you pray for persecuted believers, pray not only for what God might do for them but—as Vahid and Reza requested—for what God might do through them, for his glory. Pray for gospel fruit. Pray for Comfort and Endurance I don’t want to make prison sound easier than it was. The suffering was real. So pray also for comfort and endurance. They beat me; they broke my toe. But the prolonged separation from my two children was the hardest burden to bear. The day I went to prison, my son was 2 years old and my daughter was 7. Missing their childhoods was an unspeakable loss. Yet I know others who have suffered much more than I did. I think of a brother currently in prison who has been tortured. I think of a sister who was sexually assaulted when she was arrested. Even the apostle Paul was at times “so utterly burdened beyond [his] strength that [he] despaired of life itself.” And his request to the church was simple: “You also must help us by prayer” (2 Cor. 1:8, 11). Brothers and sisters like these need us to pray for them with love. Whatever the situation, we can pray that God would grant the suffering believer comfort, peace, and endurance. The more specific the prayers, the better. While in prison, I received letters from people around the world who were praying for me. One wrote, “I am praying for your sleep. May the Lord give you peace to sleep well in prison.” I really loved it. And honestly, I did sleep well in prison; many inmates suffered from nightmares, but I cannot remember having a single one. I believe God answered that man’s prayers. Your Prayers Reach Through Prison Walls Prayer is especially needed when a prisoner is in solitary confinement. I spent 361 days in a solitary cell: For a year, I couldn’t see the sun in the sky. Yet prayers reached me through the prison walls. I remember one day I was in cell 73. I was sitting; I wasn’t praying. Suddenly, I was able to hear, let me say, a heavenly melody in my soul—not in my ears but in my soul. And I stood up. In that moment, I was overwhelmed by joy and peace. I started dancing. The cell was only two meters by two meters, but I danced before the Lord! The guard opened the door to see what I was doing. I turned to him with a wide smile and said, “Hey, sir, how are you today?” He looked at me with big eyes. “Wow, it seems you are better than me,” he said. And then he shut the door. For a year, I couldn’t see the sun in the sky. Yet prayers reached me through the prison walls. I believe someone, or maybe a group of people, was praying for me at that time. That’s why I had the experience of hearing that melody in my soul, and I was overwhelmed by joy, even though I was in solitary confinement. Many brothers and sisters around the world prayed for me during my imprisonment. Perhaps you were one of them. I cannot find the words to say thank you. Now, I want to ask, Will you pray for those in prison right now for their faith? Scripture tells us to “remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them” (Heb. 13:3). I believe your prayer goes through the prison walls. It can touch the prisoners, encourage them, and give them joy while they’re suffering, because it’s possible to have joy and suffering at the same time. Vahid and Reza are just two of the Christians in Iran’s prisons today. There are so many. Maybe you’re asking, Where do I start? Elam’s free Bound Together resources can help your church or small group pray on the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church on November 1. We pray because our God is faithful to his children. He is faithful right now to Vahid and Reza and to all our brothers and sisters in prison. And he was faithful to me. When I came out of prison, people would say to me, “Praise God, Farshid, you were faithful to the Lord. You stood for the Lord.” I always try to correct them. That’s not true. He was faithful to me. He stood for me.

articles.content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? articles.title: The Voice of the Martyrs: Prayers of the Persecuted
articles.summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.

articles.title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
articles.content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. We pray the second petition of the Lord’s Prayer (“Thy kingdom come”) with the fifth petition also in mind (“Forgive us our debts”). Pray with a Desire for Repentance If God could turn his anger away from repentant sinners in exile (Ps. 79:5), then he could do the same for Israel’s enemies. While this is not explicit in Psalm 79, its near neighbor Psalm 83, at the conclusion of this section of Asaph psalms, prays that God would fill the faces of these enemy nations with shame “that they might seek [the LORD’s name]” (v. 16). It is legitimate to see this desire as qualifying the earlier imprecations in the Asaph collection (indeed, in the whole Psalter). Hamilton even suggests every prayer for judgment in the psalms should be read as if containing an implicit “footnote” desiring repentance as a possibility. Pray with the Hope of Final Justice The prayers of judgment, like Psalm 79, are not petty prayers incompatible with a Christian ethic. God’s people pray in response to horrific injustice, aimed at the glory of God, with a posture of humility and openness to their enemies becoming God’s friends. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. The imprecatory psalms, then, fit perfectly with the gospel of Jesus Christ. And they arm the church to intercede for the saints in a day when our Christian brothers and sisters suffer great harm throughout the world. We long for God to answer these prayers through the conversion of our enemies. But if they remain impenitent, it is only right for God to bring justice. And it is thus right for us to pray that he would.

articles.content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. What did Luther say that got his new friends so excited? In his Heidelberg Disputation , Luther described two types of people—the “theologian of glory” and the “theologian of the cross.” Theologians of glory think people are capable and smart enough to know God through human reason. They also say we can know who God’s righteous people are because we see God reward them with political power, success, and wealth. Though Luther didn’t use Albert’s and Leo’s names in his disputation, it’s clear he was talking about their greedy doctrine of indulgences when he described the theologian of glory. Luther’s “theologian of the cross,” by contrast, knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. After all, Jesus didn’t look glorious on the cross. “One deserves to be called a true theologian,” Luther wrote , “who sees God even in suffering.” As Paul wrote, “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). After Heidelberg, the phrase “ Crux sola est nostra theologia ” (“The cross alone is our theology”) became a rallying cry for Luther’s followers. It still is today. 4. Oratio, meditatio, tentatio Luther’s teaching set the Protestant Reformation in motion. In support of his reforms, Luther published hundreds of books, sermons, and hymns. Significantly, he also translated the entire Bible into the language of Germany’s common people. But Luther didn’t want common people to merely read Scripture. He wanted them to study it too. In the 1539 preface to the Wittenberg edition of his German writings, Luther wrote, “God himself lives in the Bible. Therefore, worthy Christian: get in, get in!” Luther gave his readers three rules for digging into God’s Word. Each has its own Latin term: prayer ( oratio ), meditation ( meditatio ), and suffering ( tentatio ). A ‘theologian of the cross’ knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. The first rule is kept before we read the Bible. Luther wrote, “Kneel down in your private room and with humility, pray to God to give you his Holy Spirit to enlighten and guide and give you understanding.” The second rule is kept while reading: “Read and reread the very words written down in the Bible. Observe and think about what the Holy Spirit means.” The last rule is kept when we practice what the Scriptures say. Luther said, As soon as you begin to know God’s word, the devil will afflict you. . . . This suffering will teach you how right, true, sweet, lovely, mighty, and comforting God’s word is. It is wisdom supreme. 5. Simul iustus et peccator Luther was zealous and driven. He once said, “When I want to compose, write, pray, and preach well, I must be angry.” But while anger may have given Luther energy for work, it too often burned out of control. Sadly, today, Luther is as famous for his harsh words spoken against his enemies and the Jews as he is for recovering the biblical doctrine of justification. Throughout his life, Luther taught that believers are simul iustus et peccator . That’s Latin for “simultaneously justified and a sinner.” Both realities are true of every Christian. Both were true of Luther. He was a broken man who desperately needed God’s grace, and he knew it. Luther died while visiting Eisleben on February 18, 1546. Before he died, Luther scribbled out his last written words: “We are beggars. This is true.” Luther knew he could never earn God’s grace. Salvation isn’t won through indulgences or daily prayers. This is what Luther had discovered from the Bible and taught again to the world. God sent his only Son. Christ has overcome the world. All he asks of poor, begging sinners is that we believe.
articles.content_zh: 马丁·路德于1483年11月10日生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入了曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了艾索普的"寓言". 从早年到后来在马格德堡的寄宿学校学习,路德是一名勤奋的学生。 他跟上了拉丁语,几个重要的拉丁语短语也出现在路德的著作中. 其中5个是他的生平和首席神学重心的良好总结. 1. Iustitia Dei 1505年7月,路德被猛烈的雷暴所困. 惊慌惊恐地与上帝讨价还价,许诺成为和尚. 进入修道院后,路德再次被恐惧所克服. 当他第一次作为牧师主持弥撒时, 相反,充满了颤抖。 随着礼拜的开始,路德在礼拜堂前取而代之,他开始背诵拉丁语祈祷. 路德知道上帝在判断上是完美的,并且完全没有罪恶. 因此,当他想到了iustitia Dei“上帝的公义”(1:17)时,恐怖袭击了他。 传记家罗兰·H·班顿(Roland H. Bainton)描述了困扰路德思想的思想:我该向神圣的陛下举起手来, 众天神围绕他. 在他点头的时候,大地会颤抖... ...但是,我是灰尘和灰烬。 当路德拿起面包和葡萄酒时,他摇得这么厉害,差点把杯子掉下. 在那些年里,路德在学校和修道院里长大,他只把上帝的正义或正义视为他对人类罪恶的积极判断。 他后来写道, 虽然我作为一个和尚生活 没有责备, 我感觉和知道我是上帝面前的罪人。 我有一个极度不安的良心。 我憎恨惩罚罪人的善良之神 2. 1512年,路德成为维滕贝格的大学教授. 当他为他的演讲而学习圣经时,他开始在新的光芒下看到上帝的正义. 路德看到耶稣基督如何对待我们的人性,他如何过上完美的生活并死于十字架上的痛苦而可耻的死亡来取取罪的惩罚. 他看见了上帝如何使耶稣从死地复活,以及他现在如何通过信仰为基督徒辩护. 上帝宣布,在他看来,耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的救赎天赋。 耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡是所有信徒的计数. 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的天赋。 当路德做出这个发现时发生了什么? 他是这样描述的 : “ 我感到我再次出生,并通过开放的大门进入了天堂。 ” 在那一天之后,路德开始教导上帝给予基督徒“外星人的正义 ” , 即“来自我们以外的”一种格外不义的正义。 我们的正义不是来自我们, 祈祷, 我们的正义最终被发现 并属于另一个,我们的救主耶稣基督。 3. Crux sola est nostra Godologia 1517年10月31日,路德将他的"95个本事"出名地贴在了城堡教堂的门上. 路德在书中明确表示反对教皇利奥十世和德国自己的勃兰登堡阿尔贝特亲王赞助的集资宽恕计划。 次年,即1518年4月,路德在海德堡举行的奥古斯丁会令春季会议上为这些观点辩护. 路德在恐惧中走去开会. 他期望那里的领导人严厉斥责他。 这毕竟是教皇要求他们做的。 但令路德惊讶的是,与会领导人激动地欢迎他的辩护. 路德怎么说 他的新朋友这么兴奋? 路德在他的"海德堡争论"中描述了两类人——"荣耀之神"和"十字架之神". 荣耀的神学家们认为,人的能力和智慧足以通过人类理性来认识上帝. 他们也说,我们可以知道上帝的善良人民是谁,因为我们看到真主以政治力量、成功和财富奖励他们。 虽然路德在争论中并没有使用阿尔伯特和利奥的名字,但很明显,当他描述荣耀的神学家时,他在谈论他们贪婪的宽恕理论。 相对而言,路德的“十字架神学家”知道,并非总能让世界标准显示良好、美丽和强大的人真正了解上帝。 毕竟耶稣在十字架上并不光荣。 路德写道 : “ 一个人应该被称为真正的神学家,” 路德写道,“谁在痛苦中看到上帝。 ” 正如保罗所写道的:“上帝选择了世界上的愚蠢来羞辱智者;上帝选择了世界上的弱者来羞辱强者。” 海德堡之后, " Crux sola est nostra Godologia " ( " 十字架是我们的神学 " )成为路德信徒的呼声。 今天还是这样。 4. Oratio、meditatio、tentatio Luther的教义使新教改革运动开始。 为支持他的改革,路德出版了上百本书,布道,并作"赞". 重要的是,他还将整个"圣经"翻译成了德国普通人的语言. 但路德并不想普通人只读圣经。 他希望他们也研究它。 路德在他的德文著作"维滕贝格"1539年版的前言中写道:"上帝自己活在圣经中. 因此,值得的基督徒:上车,上车!” 路德给了读者三条钻入上帝之道的规则. 每个词都有自己的拉丁名词:祷告(oratio),冥想(meditatio)和苦难(tentatio). 一个“十字架的神学家”知道,并非总有人以世界标准看起来是好人、美丽人和强大的人真正了解上帝。 第一条规则在我们读出"圣经"之前被保留. 路德写道:“跪在你的私人房间里谦逊地祈祷真主赐予你他的圣灵以启蒙、引导和谅解。” 第二条规则在读取时保留:“读取并重读圣经所写的文字。 观察并思考圣灵的意义。” 最后一个规则是当我们实践圣经所说的话时, 路德说,一旦你明白上帝的话,恶魔就会折磨你。 这种痛苦将教你如何正确、真实、甜蜜、可爱、强大并安慰上帝的话。 智慧至高无上。 5. Simul iustus et peccator Luther是狂热和有动力的。 他曾经说过:“当我想写作、写作、祈祷和讲道的时候,我一定生气了。” 但是,虽然愤怒可能已经让路德精力充沛地工作,但是它经常被烧得失控. 可悲的是,今天,路德以其对敌人和犹太人的严酷言辞而出名,如同他收复了圣经中的辩解学说而出名. 路德一生教导信徒们, 这在拉丁语中是“极端合理和有罪者 ” 。 每个基督教徒都一样 路德也一样 他是一个破碎的人,他迫切需要上帝的恩惠,他知道这一点。 1546年2月18日路德在访问艾斯莱本时去世. 在他死前,路德写出他最后的文字:“我们是乞丐。 这是事实。” Luther知道他永远得不到上帝的恩惠。 救赎不是通过宽容或日常祈祷而赢得的。 这是路德从圣经中发现的,并再次向世界传授. 上帝派他唯一的儿子 基督战胜了这个世界 他只要求贫穷 乞求罪人 我们相信
